questions.label: Hard
body: For m=2, consider f(x)=(x-2)<sup>2</sup>(x+4). The investigation connects factorization, stationary points and Newton's method.
questions.title: A polynomial with a repeated root

parts.label: a
parts.html: Expand f(x) and hence write it in the form x<sup>3</sup>+ax+b.

parts.label: b
parts.html: State all roots with their multiplicities and explain how the graph behaves at each root.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the stationary points and classify each one.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Derive the Newton-Raphson iteration for solving f(x)=0.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Starting with x<sub>0</sub>=-6.4, calculate x<sub>1</sub> through x<sub>4</sub>.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Explain why Newton's method converges more slowly near the repeated root than near the simple root, and give a modification that restores faster convergence.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Expanding gives f(x)=x3-12x+16.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: The roots are x=2, multiplicity 2, and x=-4, multiplicity 1. The graph touches the axis at x=2 and crosses it at x=-4.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: f'(x)=3x²-12=3(x-2)(x+2). Thus x=±2. f(-2)=32 and f(2)=0. Since f''(x)=6x, (-2,32) is a local maximum and (2,0) is a local minimum.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html:
Using xn+1=xn-f(xn)/f'(xn),
xn+1=xn-[(xn-2)²(xn+4)]/[3xn²-12].

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: The iterates are x1=-4.87, x2=-4.18, x3=-4.01, x4=-4. They approach -4.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: At x=2, both f and f' vanish, so the ordinary iteration has only linear convergence. For a double root use xn+1=xn-2f(xn)/f'(xn), which restores quadratic convergence when started sufficiently close.

questions.label: Hard
body: A response is modelled for x≥0 by R(x)=x²e<sup>-x/2</sup>. The model rises from zero and then decays.
questions.title: A peaked exponential model

parts.label: a
parts.html: Find R'(x) in factorized form.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Find the coordinates of the non-zero maximum point.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the two positive x-values at which the response is half its maximum.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Evaluate the total response ∫ from 0 to infinity of R(x) dx.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the mean x-coordinate if R is normalized to form a probability density.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Compare the mode and mean and explain the direction of skewness suggested by the model.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: By the product rule, R'(x)=e-x/2x(2-x/2).

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: For x>0, R'(x)=0 gives x=2k=4. The derivative changes from positive to negative, so the maximum is (4,2.17).

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Solve x²e-x/2=1.08 graphically or numerically. The solutions are x≈1.52 and x≈8.31.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Using ∫₀∞x²e-axdx=2/a³ with a=1/2, the integral is 2k³=16.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: The normalizing integral is 2k³. Also ∫₀∞x³e-x/kdx=6k⁴. Hence E(X)=6k⁴/(2k³)=3k=6.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: The mode is 2k=4 and the mean is 3k=6. Since the mean lies to the right of the mode and the model has a long right tail, it is positively skewed.

parts.label: b

solparts.label: b

solparts.label: f

questions.label: Hard
body: A quantity satisfies u<sub>0</sub>=80 and u<sub>n+1</sub>=0.55u<sub>n</sub>+12.
questions.title: A convergent recurrence

parts.label: a
parts.html: Calculate u1, u2 and u3.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Find the equilibrium value L and explain why the sequence converges to it.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Show by induction that u_n=L+(u0-L)r^n.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find u<sub>12</sub>.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the sum u0+u1+...+u<sub>11</sub>.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Find the least n for which |u_n-L|<0.01 and justify the logarithmic inequality used.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Successive substitution gives u1=56, u2=42.8, u3=35.5.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Set L=0.55L+12. Thus L=26.7. Since |0.55|<1, deviations from L are multiplied by 0.55 each step, so they tend to zero.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html:
At n=0 the formula gives u0. Assuming it holds at n,
un+1=r[L+(u0-L)rⁿ]+c=rL+c+(u0-L)rⁿ⁺¹=L+(u0-L)rⁿ⁺¹. Hence the result holds for all n≥0.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Substitute n=12: u12=26.7+(80-26.7)(0.55)12≈26.7.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Sum the closed form: 12L+(u0-L)(1-r12)/(1-r)≈438.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: We need |u0-L|rⁿ<0.01. Thus n ln r<ln(0.01/|u0-L|). Because ln r<0, division reverses the inequality. Hence n>14.4, so take the next integer.

body: A continuous random variable X has density f(x)=Cx<sup>1</sup> for 0≤x≤4, and f(x)=0 otherwise.
questions.title: A power-law probability density

parts.label: a
parts.html: Find the exact value of C.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Find the cumulative distribution function on 0≤x≤L.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find P(X>0.8L).

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find the mean and variance of X.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the median of X.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Let Y=(X/L)^(p+1). Determine the distribution of Y.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Normalization gives C·42/(2)=1. Hence C=(2)/16.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: F(x)=∫₀ˣCt1dt=Cx2/(2)=(x/4)2.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: E(X)=CL3/(3)=2.67. E(X²)=CL4/(4)=8. Thus Var(X)=0.889.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Set F(m)=0.5: (m/4)2=0.5. Hence m=4(0.5)1/2≈2.83.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: For 0≤y≤1, P(Y≤y)=P(X≤L y1/(p+1))=F(L y1/(p+1))=y. Therefore Y is uniform on [0,1].

questions.label: Hard
body: A population P(t) satisfies dP/dt=0.18P(1-P/800) with P(0)=80.
questions.title: Logistic growth

parts.label: a
parts.html: State the equilibrium solutions and describe their stability for positive populations.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Separate variables and obtain the general logistic form P=K/(1+Ae^(-kt)).

parts.label: c
parts.html: Use the initial condition to find A.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find the time at which the population first reaches 75% of carrying capacity.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the time and value of the maximum growth rate.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Use one Euler step of width 1 from t=0 and compare it with the exact value at t=1.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Equilibria satisfy P(1-P/800)=0, so P=0 and P=800. For 0<P<800, dP/dt>0; above 800, dP/dt<0. Thus 800 is stable and 0 is unstable for positive perturbations.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Using partial fractions, ∫[1/P+1/(K-P)]dP=k dt. Hence ln(P/(K-P))=kt+C, which rearranges to P=K/(1+Ae-kt).

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: 80=800/(1+A), so A=9.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Set P=0.75K. Then Ae-kt=1/3, so t=ln(3A)/k≈18.3.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: kP(1-P/K) is a downward quadratic in P, maximized at P=K/2=400.0. This occurs when Ae-kt=1, so t=ln A/k≈12.2. Maximum rate=kK/4≈36.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: Euler: P1=80+0.18(80)(1-80/800)≈93. Exact P(1)≈93.9. The one-step error is about -0.965.

questions.label: Hard
body: Define S<sub>n</sub>(θ)=Σ from k=1 to n of cos(kθ). Take n=6 and θ=π/5 for numerical parts.
questions.title: A trigonometric sum

parts.label: a
parts.html: Write Σ e^(ikθ) as a finite geometric series.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Derive S_n(θ)=sin(nθ/2)cos((n+1)θ/2)/sin(θ/2).

parts.label: c
parts.html: Evaluate S_n(θ) for the specified n and θ.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find all θ in (0,2π) for which S_n(θ)=0, excluding values that make the derived denominator zero.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find lim as θ approaches 0 of S_n(θ).

parts.label: f
parts.html: Interpret the complex sum geometrically and explain when its magnitude is small.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html:
With ratio eiθ, Σk=1
neikθ=eiθ(1-einθ)/(1-eiθ).

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Rewrite 1-e<sup>inθ</sup>=-2ie<sup>inθ/2</sup>sin(nθ/2) and similarly for the denominator. Taking the real part gives the stated formula.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Substitution gives S≈-1.81. Direct summation gives -1.81, confirming the result.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: The numerator is zero when sin(nθ/2)=0 or cos((n+1)θ/2)=0. Thus θ=2πj/6 or θ=(2j+1)π/7, retaining values in (0,2π) and checking overlaps; θ=0,2π are excluded.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Each cos(kθ) tends to 1, so the sum tends to n=6. The formula agrees because sin(nθ/2)/sin(θ/2)→n and cos((n+1)θ/2)→1.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: The terms are unit vectors with arguments θ,2θ,...,nθ. Their vector sum is the diagonal of the resulting polygonal chain. Its magnitude is small when the directions are spread nearly symmetrically around the circle, causing cancellation.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Find the acute angle between l and Π.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the perpendicular distance from A to Π.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find the foot H of the perpendicular from A to Π.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the reflection A' of A in Π.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Find the equation of the sphere centred at A and tangent to Π, and state its point of tangency.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Substitution gives 3+3t=9, so t=2. Therefore I=(3, 4, -1).

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Distance=|3-9|/√(1²+2²+2²)=6/3=2.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html:
Move from A in the normal direction: H=A+λn. Since n·H=9, λ=(9-3)/9=2/3. Hence
H=(1.67,1.33,2.33).

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: H is the midpoint of AA'. Therefore A'=2H-A=(2.33,2.67,3.67).

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: The radius equals the distance from A to Π, namely 2. Thus (x-1)²+y²+(z-1)²=4, tangent at H=(1.67,1.33,2.33).

questions.label: Hard
body: The function f(x)=e<sup>-x</sup> is approximated using its Maclaurin series. For a numerical check take x=0.3.
questions.title: A Maclaurin approximation

parts.label: a
parts.html: Find the Maclaurin polynomial of degree 4.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Use P4 to approximate the specified value of e^(-x).

parts.label: c
parts.html: Give a valid upper bound for the absolute error using the next term or Taylor's theorem.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Use P4 to approximate ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(-x) dx.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Compare the approximation with the exact integral and calculate the percentage error.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Explain how the degree required for a fixed accuracy changes as |x| grows.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Since f(k)(0)=(-1)k, P4(x)=1-x+x²/2-x³/6+x⁴/24.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: P4(0.3)=0.741, while the calculator value is 0.741.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: For x>0 the alternating terms decrease here, so the error is at most x⁵/120≈2.02e-05. The actual error is 1.93e-05.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Integrating term by term gives 1-1/2+1/6-1/24+1/120=0.633.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: The exact integral is 1-e-1≈0.632. Percentage error≈0.192%.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: For a fixed degree, omitted terms generally grow with |x|. To maintain the same accuracy farther from the expansion point, more terms are required. Range reduction or expansion about a nearer point can improve efficiency.

questions.label: Hard
body: Let a<sub>n</sub> be the number of binary strings of length n containing no two consecutive 1s.
questions.title: Binary strings without consecutive ones

parts.label: a
parts.html: Find a1, a2 and a3 by listing or direct reasoning.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Show that a_n=a_(n-1)+a_(n-2).

parts.label: c
parts.html: Calculate a<sub>10</sub>.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Solve the recurrence using the characteristic equation.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the probability that a uniformly chosen binary string of length 10 has no consecutive 1s.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Find lim a_(n+1)/a_n and interpret it.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: A valid string ending in 0 can follow any valid length n-1 string. A valid string ending in 1 must end in 01, preceded by any valid length n-2 string. The cases are disjoint, giving the recurrence.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Starting with a0=1 and a1=2 and iterating gives a10=144.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: The characteristic equation r²=r+1 has roots φ=(1+√5)/2 and ψ=(1-√5)/2. Matching the initial values gives an=(φn+2-ψn+2)/√5.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: There are 210 binary strings in total, so the probability is 144/210≈0.141.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: Since |ψ|<1<φ, the φ term dominates. Therefore the ratio tends to φ≈1.62, the long-run multiplication factor for the count.
